documents.title: UPI payment failures
documents.body:
## Why a UPI collect request can fail

A UPI collect request routed through payment-service can fail for a handful of
reasons, and the error code Ledgerly logs tells you which one:

- **ERR_UPI_COLLECT_FAILED** — the customer's bank declined the request outright.
  This usually means insufficient balance, an incorrect UPI PIN entered too many
  times, or the receiving VPA being temporarily suspended by the PSP.
- **ERR_UPI_COLLECT_EXPIRED** — the customer did not approve the request within
  the UPI-mandated window (typically 2 minutes on most apps). The request must
  be raised again; it cannot be resurrected.

## Reversal timeline

Payments that are debited from the customer's account without a corresponding
order being marked paid on the Ledgerly side are automatically detected by the
nightly reconciliation job and reversed by the PSP within **5–7 business days**.
This is not a Ledgerly-controlled window; it is set by the NPCI dispute
resolution process that every UPI-enabled PSP must follow.

## What to tell the customer

If a customer reports money left their account but Ledgerly still shows the
order as unpaid, confirm the UPI reference number (a 12-digit UTR) and check
whether ERR_UPI_COLLECT_FAILED or ERR_SETTLEMENT_DELAY appears against the
transaction in payment-service's logs. If neither appears and the debit is
confirmed, the reversal is already in progress and the 5–7 business day window
applies from the debit date, not from the date the customer contacts support.

documents.title: Manual reversal process
documents.body:
## When a manual reversal is needed

The automatic reconciliation job in payment-service catches the overwhelming
majority of failed-but-debited UPI payments. A manual reversal is only needed
when the automatic job has not picked up the transaction after 7 business days,
or when the customer disputes the amount reversed.

## Requesting one

An agent can request a manual reversal by sharing the customer's UPI reference
number (UTR) with the payments operations team via the internal reversal queue.
The UTR is a 12-digit number visible in the customer's bank statement and in
payment-service's transaction log against the same order.

## What happens after

Once submitted, payment-service opens a dispute case with the PSP directly.
This typically resolves within 3 additional business days beyond the standard
window, because it skips the automated reconciliation cycle. The customer
should be told the manual path is the exception, not the default — most
reversals never need it.

documents.title: Settlement delays
documents.body:
## What ERR_SETTLEMENT_DELAY means

Settlement is the process by which money collected via UPI, cards or netbanking
actually lands in the merchant's bank account, distinct from the collection
itself succeeding. ERR_SETTLEMENT_DELAY appears in payment-service's logs when
a batch of collected payments has not settled within the PSP's stated SLA,
typically T+2 working days.

## Common causes

- A bank holiday extending the settlement window (settlement only happens on
  working days for the receiving bank, not the paying one).
- The PSP's own settlement batch running late — this is visible on the PSP's
  status page and is outside Ledgerly's control.
- An account-level hold placed by the PSP pending KYC re-verification.

## Communicating with the customer

Settlement delay is not the same as payment failure. The customer has already
been charged; the money is in transit to the merchant's account. Reassure them
the payment succeeded and give the T+2 (or T+3 across a bank holiday) figure
rather than an open-ended "we're looking into it," which reads as uncertainty
about something that is actually well understood.

documents.title: Gateway timeouts and 5xx errors
documents.body:
## ERR_GATEWAY_5XX

When the payment gateway itself returns a 5xx error mid-transaction, the
outcome is genuinely ambiguous from the customer's side: the money may or may
not have been debited, because the failure could have happened before or after
the bank processed it.

## The safe response

Never tell a customer a gateway-5xx transaction definitely failed. Check
payment-service's transaction log for a matching entry with status PENDING or
FAILED. A PENDING entry older than 15 minutes should be treated as failed and
the customer should retry; a FAILED entry means no debit occurred and no
refund is needed, because none was taken.

## Timeout versus decline

ERR_PAY_TIMEOUT (the gateway never responded within the configured window) and
ERR_PAY_DECLINED (the gateway responded, and the bank said no) are different
failure modes with different next steps. A timeout is safe to retry
immediately. A decline should not be retried without the customer checking
their bank app first — most declines are insufficient balance or a blocked
card, and an immediate retry just fails the same way again.

documents.title: Refund processing timeline
documents.body:
## ERR_REFUND_PENDING and normal refund timing

A refund initiated through Ledgerly typically takes 5–7 business days to
reflect in the customer's account once approved, matching the UPI reversal
timeline because refunds and reversals both go through the same PSP settlement
rails. ERR_REFUND_PENDING in payment-service's log is not an error in the
everyday sense — it is the normal status for a refund that has been approved
but has not yet cleared the bank's processing window.

## When to escalate

A refund still showing ERR_REFUND_PENDING after 10 business days (beyond the
normal window with margin) should be escalated to payments operations with the
refund reference number. Before escalating, confirm the customer is checking
the correct account — refunds to a UPI-linked account return to the original
payment method, which is not always the account balance the customer expects
if they paid via a linked card.

documents.title: Duplicate charge detection
documents.body:
## How Ledgerly prevents double-charging

Every payment request from the Ledgerly client carries an idempotency key.
payment-service rejects a second request with the same key within a 24-hour
window with ERR_IDEMPOTENCY_CONFLICT rather than processing it twice — this is
the mechanism that makes a customer's accidental double-tap on "Pay" safe.

## What a genuine duplicate looks like

A genuine duplicate charge — two separate successful debits for what the
customer intended as one payment — almost always means two different
idempotency keys were used, typically because the customer's connection
dropped between the first attempt appearing to fail and them retrying.

## Resolving a confirmed duplicate

Confirm both transaction UTRs are distinct and both show SUCCESS in
payment-service. If confirmed, the second (later) transaction is refunded in
full, following the standard refund timeline. The first transaction is left
untouched as the transaction of record.

documents.title: Payment method troubleshooting
documents.body:
## Card, UPI and netbanking failure patterns

Different payment methods fail for different reasons, and matching the pattern
to the method rules out the wrong root cause quickly.

**Cards** most often fail on ERR_PAY_DECLINED from the issuing bank —
insufficient limit, an international-transaction block, or 3D-Secure OTP
expiry. Card failures rarely relate to Ledgerly's own systems.

**UPI** failures are usually ERR_UPI_COLLECT_FAILED (declined) or
ERR_UPI_COLLECT_EXPIRED (not approved in time) — see the dedicated UPI article
for the reversal timeline that applies to a failed-but-debited case.

**Netbanking** failures are the rarest and, when they happen, are almost
always ERR_GATEWAY_5XX from the bank's own netbanking gateway rather than
anything payment-service controls.

## The one question that resolves most cases quickly

"Did your bank send you an SMS or notification about this transaction?" A yes
means the bank attempted the debit and the outcome is on their side to
confirm; a no means the request likely never reached the bank and a clean
retry is the right next step.

documents.title: Investigating a stuck UPI payment
documents.body:
## Procedure

1. Pull the transaction record from payment-service by order id or UTR.
2. Check `status`. `PENDING` older than 15 minutes: treat as stuck.
   `FAILED`: no customer-facing action beyond explaining the decline reason.
   `SUCCESS` with the order still unpaid: this is a reconciliation lag, not a
   stuck payment — check the nightly reconciliation job's last run time first.
3. For a genuinely stuck `PENDING` transaction, do not manually mark it paid.
   File a ticket with payments operations quoting the UTR; they query the PSP
   directly, which agents do not have access to do.
4. Log every stuck-payment investigation in the internal ops channel with the
   UTR, even if it resolves itself — the pattern across many "resolved itself"
   cases is what eventually gets a flaky PSP integration fixed.

## What not to do

Never issue a refund for a `PENDING` transaction. If it later clears as
`SUCCESS`, the customer has been refunded for a successful payment, which is a
much harder mistake to unwind than a delayed answer.

documents.title: Escalating a PSP-side settlement dispute
documents.body:
## When this runbook applies

Use this when a merchant disputes a settlement amount, not a customer disputing
a charge — those are different tickets with different owners (BILLING and
PAYMENT respectively) even though both eventually touch payment-service.

## Steps

1. Export the settlement batch report for the disputed date range from
   payment-service's admin panel.
2. Cross-reference against the PSP's own settlement report, available from the
   PSP's merchant dashboard (credentials in the ops vault, not agent-accessible
   — request from a team lead).
3. A discrepancy under ₹500 across a batch is typically a rounding artefact in
   fee calculation and self-resolves at the next settlement cycle.
4. A discrepancy over ₹500, or any recurring discrepancy, gets escalated to the
   PSP's merchant support with both reports attached. Expect a 5-business-day
   response time from the PSP.
5. Never promise the merchant a specific resolution date for a PSP-side
   dispute — Ledgerly does not control the PSP's investigation timeline.

documents.title: Understanding your Ledgerly invoice
documents.body:
## What appears on a Ledgerly invoice

A Ledgerly subscription invoice lists the plan tier (FREE, PRO or ENTERPRISE),
the billing period, any add-ons, and — for a PRO or ENTERPRISE plan billed
annually — the prorated adjustment if the plan changed mid-cycle.

## Reading a proration line

A proration line with a negative amount is a credit for time unused on the
previous plan; a positive amount is the additional charge for the new plan's
remaining period. Both are calculated to the day, not the month, so a plan
change on the 17th of a 30-day cycle prorates 13/30ths of the difference.

## Tax and GST

Every invoice includes GST at the applicable rate for the customer's
registered state. A customer disputing the GST amount should be asked to
confirm their GSTIN is current in account settings — an outdated or missing
GSTIN is the most common cause of an unexpected tax line.

documents.title: Plan downgrade blocked
documents.body:
## ERR_PLAN_DOWNGRADE_BLOCKED

Ledgerly blocks a downgrade from PRO or ENTERPRISE to a lower tier when the
account is currently using a feature the target tier does not support — most
commonly more team members than FREE allows, or more than one connected bank
feed on a plan that only supports one.

## Resolving it

The invoice or account page names the specific blocking condition. The
customer needs to remove the excess team members, disconnect the extra bank
feed, or otherwise bring usage within the target plan's limits before the
downgrade can proceed. Ledgerly does not automatically remove data or
disconnect integrations on a customer's behalf, because that decision belongs
to the customer.

## What downgrading does not affect

Historical data, past invoices and exported reports are retained regardless of
plan tier. A downgrade only affects what can be created or connected going
forward, never what already exists.

documents.title: Card on file expired
documents.body:
## ERR_CARD_ON_FILE_EXPIRED

Ledgerly attempts to charge the card on file three days before a subscription
renewal. If the card has expired, this fails with ERR_CARD_ON_FILE_EXPIRED and
the customer receives an email prompting them to update their payment method.

## Grace period

The subscription remains active for a 7-day grace period from the failed
charge, during which the customer can update their card and the renewal will
retry automatically overnight. After 7 days with no successful charge, the
account is downgraded to FREE — not suspended, and no data is lost.

## Reactivating

Once the customer updates their card, ask them to trigger the retry manually
from the billing page rather than waiting for the overnight job, if they want
their PRO features back the same day.

documents.title: Subscription plan comparison
documents.body:
## FREE, PRO and ENTERPRISE

FREE supports one team member, one connected bank feed, and core invoicing.
PRO adds unlimited team members, up to five bank feeds, GST return filing, and
priority support routing. ENTERPRISE adds unlimited bank feeds, a dedicated
account manager, and SLA-backed support response times.

## Choosing between PRO and ENTERPRISE

The deciding factor is almost always bank-feed count and support SLA
requirements rather than any individual feature — most PRO features are
available on ENTERPRISE too, and ENTERPRISE is priced for businesses that need
the guaranteed response time more than any specific capability.

## Trial periods

A 14-day PRO trial is available once per account, starting from first
activation. It cannot be repeated by downgrading and re-upgrading; the trial
flag is set permanently on the account, not on the current subscription
state.

documents.title: Invoice payment methods
documents.body:
## How Ledgerly charges for its own subscription

Ledgerly's own subscription invoices (as opposed to the customer's payments to
their own customers, handled by payment-service) are charged via card only —
UPI and netbanking are not supported for subscription billing, only for the
customer's own collections through the product.

## Updating the card on file

The card on file for subscription billing is managed separately from any card
saved for other purposes. A customer confused about "why did my card get
charged for Ledgerly" versus a payment collected through Ledgerly should be
shown the distinction: subscription charges appear with the merchant name
"LEDGERLY SUBSCRIPTION", collected payments show the customer's own business
name.

documents.title: GST invoice corrections
documents.body:
## When a GST invoice needs correcting

An incorrect GSTIN, business name or address on a past Ledgerly subscription
invoice can be corrected by support, but only going forward — a GST invoice,
once issued, cannot be edited retroactively under GST rules. Instead, a credit
note is issued for the incorrect invoice and a fresh one is generated with the
corrected details.

## What the customer needs to provide

The corrected GSTIN (verified against the GST portal format: 15 characters,
state code first two digits), the correct legal business name matching GST
registration, and the correct registered address. Support cannot accept a
trade name in place of the GST-registered legal name.

documents.title: Processing a billing credit note
documents.body:
## When to issue one

A credit note is issued when a past subscription invoice needs correcting
(GST details, an incorrectly applied proration) or when a goodwill credit is
approved for a service disruption.

## Steps

1. Confirm the original invoice number and the exact amount to credit.
2. For a GST correction, the credit note must reference the original invoice
   number per GST compliance rules — never issue a standalone credit for a GST
   correction.
3. For a goodwill credit, team-lead approval is required above ₹2,000; below
   that, any agent may issue it directly from the billing admin panel.
4. The credit is applied to the next invoice automatically; it is not paid out
   as cash or a bank transfer under any circumstance.

documents.title: Handling a disputed subscription charge
documents.body:
## Procedure

1. Pull the subscription's billing history and confirm the disputed charge
   matches an actual renewal or plan-change event — check for
   ERR_PRORATION_MISMATCH in the billing log, which flags a proration
   calculated against a stale plan snapshot.
2. If ERR_PRORATION_MISMATCH appears, the charge is incorrect by construction
   and should be corrected via a credit note (see the credit note runbook)
   without further investigation.
3. If no error is logged and the charge matches a plan the account was
   genuinely on, explain the charge using the plan comparison and invoice
   articles rather than crediting by default — most disputes are a
   misunderstanding of proration, not a billing bug.
4. Escalate to a team lead only when the customer disputes a charge that both
   matches the account's plan history and has no logged discrepancy — that is
   the case actually worth a second pair of eyes.

documents.title: Password reset not arriving
documents.body:
## Why a reset email might not arrive

The most common causes, in order of frequency: the email landed in spam or a
promotions tab, the customer is checking an inbox different from the one
registered on the account, or — rarely — auth-service's outbound mail queue is
delayed.

## What to check first

Ask the customer to search their inbox (including spam) for "Ledgerly" rather
than scrolling, and confirm the email address they are checking matches the
one on the account exactly — a common failure is a customer with two email
addresses checking the wrong one.

## If genuinely not delivered

auth-service logs every reset email dispatch with a delivery status. If the
dispatch log shows SENT but the customer has confirmed they checked spam and
the right inbox, request a fresh reset — reset links expire after 30 minutes,
and a customer troubleshooting for a while may simply need a new one.

documents.title: Two-factor authentication issues
documents.body:
## ERR_2FA_MISMATCH

This appears when the six-digit code the customer entered does not match what
auth-service's TOTP validator expects for that moment. The most common cause
by far is the customer's phone clock being out of sync — TOTP codes are
time-based and a phone more than 30 seconds off will generate wrong codes
consistently.

## Resolving it

Ask the customer to check their phone's date and time are set to automatic
rather than manual. If codes still mismatch after that, the authenticator app
may have been set up against a different account or re-installed without
re-scanning the QR code, which silently generates a different code sequence.

## Resetting 2FA

Resetting 2FA requires identity verification beyond a normal support
interaction — see the 2FA reset runbook. Agents should never disable 2FA on a
customer's say-so alone.

documents.title: Session expiry and unexpected logouts
documents.body:
## Normal session length

A Ledgerly session lasts 24 hours of inactivity, or until the browser's
storage is cleared, whichever comes first. Being logged out after exactly that
window is expected behaviour, not a bug.

## ERR_SESSION_REVOKED

This specific error means the session was invalidated deliberately — most
often because the customer (or someone with access to their account) changed
the password, which auth-service treats as "log out every other active
session" as a security measure. A customer reporting frequent unexpected
logouts should be asked whether they changed their password recently, or
whether anyone else has account access.

## Frequent logouts with no password change

If sessions are ending well inside the 24-hour window and no password change
occurred, check whether the customer uses aggressive browser privacy settings
or an extension that clears cookies — this is a browser-side behaviour, not
something auth-service does.

documents.title: API key management
documents.body:
## Creating and revoking API keys

API keys are created from the developer settings page and are shown in full
exactly once, at creation. Ledgerly does not store the raw key — only a hash —
so a lost key cannot be recovered and must be revoked and replaced.

## ERR_APIKEY_REVOKED

This means the specific key used in a request has been revoked, either
deliberately by an admin or automatically after auth-service detected the key
being used from an unrecognised IP range that the account's security policy
does not allow.

## Key rotation

Rotating a key (revoking the old one and issuing a new one) does not require
downtime if the integration is updated to use the new key before the old one
is revoked — Ledgerly supports both keys being valid simultaneously for up to
1 hour to allow a clean cutover.

documents.title: Login troubleshooting checklist
documents.body:
## Before escalating a login issue

1. Confirm the customer is using the correct tenant — Ledgerly accounts are
   tenant-scoped, and a customer with access to multiple businesses on
   Ledgerly must select the right one at login, not just enter credentials.
2. Confirm the password itself, not just that "login isn't working" — ask them
   to try a password reset rather than guessing at the actual symptom.
3. Check auth-service's login attempt log for the account: repeated
   ERR_AUTH_TOKEN_EXPIRED entries suggest a client-side clock or caching
   issue; repeated failed-password entries suggest the customer genuinely has
   the wrong password.

## When it is not a Ledgerly issue

A customer who can log in from a phone but not a laptop (or vice versa) almost
always has a browser extension, corporate firewall, or cached credentials
issue on the failing device — this is rarely something auth-service logs will
explain, because the request may never be reaching Ledgerly at all.

documents.title: Understanding auth token expiry
documents.body:
## ERR_AUTH_TOKEN_EXPIRED

Ledgerly's access tokens are short-lived by design — 15 minutes — and are
silently refreshed in the background by the client as long as the underlying
session is valid. This error surfacing to a customer means the refresh itself
failed, not that their login expired in the everyday sense.

## Common causes

A refresh failure usually means the customer's device clock is significantly
wrong (the token's validity window is time-based), or a browser extension is
blocking the background refresh request specifically while allowing the main
page to load normally.

## What resolves it

A full logout and login back in obtains a fresh token pair and resolves the
symptom in essentially all cases. This is different from merely refreshing
the page, which does not force a new token exchange.

documents.title: Verifying identity before a 2FA reset
documents.body:
## Why this exists

2FA exists specifically to prevent account takeover. Resetting it on request
without verification defeats the purpose entirely — an attacker's most direct
path into an account is convincing support to remove the second factor.

## Required verification, all three

1. The email address on file, confirmed by the customer replying from it (not
   stated in chat).
2. The last four digits of the payment card on file, OR the exact amount of
   the most recent Ledgerly subscription invoice.
3. A photo of a government ID matching the legal name on the account, for
   PRO/ENTERPRISE accounts only — FREE accounts skip this step given the lower
   stakes.

## After verification

Reset 2FA from the admin panel, which immediately invalidates the old
authenticator pairing and forces the customer through fresh QR-code setup on
next login. Log the verification method used in the account's security notes
— this record is what protects the agent if the reset is later disputed.

documents.title: Investigating repeated ERR_SESSION_REVOKED reports
documents.body:
## Steps

1. Check the account's password change history for a timestamp matching the
   customer's report of being logged out.
2. If a password change matches, this is expected behaviour — explain it and
   close.
3. If no password change occurred, check for any admin-initiated session
   revocation (visible in the tenant's audit log) — a team lead or admin on
   the account may have revoked sessions deliberately, including their own by
   mistake.
4. If neither explains it, escalate to platform engineering with the account
   id and timestamps — an unexplained mass session revocation with no
   corresponding action in the audit log is a signal worth investigating
   rather than explaining away.

documents.title: Rate limiting and ERR_RATE_LIMIT
documents.body:
## Current limits

api-gateway enforces 100 requests per minute per API key on PRO, and 500 per
minute on ENTERPRISE. FREE-tier accounts do not have API access at all.

## Diagnosing an unexpected rate limit

A customer hitting ERR_RATE_LIMIT while believing they are well under the
documented limit is very often making requests from multiple processes or
servers sharing one API key — the limit is per key, not per calling process,
so five workers each making 30 requests a minute against the same key hit the
PRO limit collectively even though none of them individually would.

## Response headers

Every api-gateway response includes RateLimit-Limit, RateLimit-Remaining and
RateLimit-Reset headers so an integration can self-throttle before hitting the
limit rather than discovering it by trial and error. Point developers at these
headers before assuming a limit increase is needed.

documents.title: Webhook delivery failures
documents.body:
## ERR_WEBHOOK_DELIVERY_FAILED

api-gateway retries a failed webhook delivery with exponential backoff for up
to 24 hours before giving up and marking it permanently failed. A delivery is
considered failed if the receiving endpoint does not return a 2xx status
within 10 seconds.

## Common customer-side causes

The receiving endpoint returning a non-2xx status because of an unrelated bug
on the customer's own server, the endpoint being behind a firewall that blocks
Ledgerly's outbound IP range, or a slow endpoint that exceeds the 10-second
timeout under load.

## Manual redelivery

Webhook events remain available for manual redelivery from the developer
dashboard for 30 days after the original attempt, so once a customer fixes the
receiving-side issue, historical events are not lost — they simply need to be
manually replayed.

documents.title: API idempotency keys
documents.body:
## Why every write request needs one

Every POST to the Ledgerly API that creates or modifies a resource requires an
Idempotency-Key header. Retrying a request with the same key returns the
original response without creating a duplicate; the same key with a different
body returns ERR_IDEMPOTENCY_CONFLICT.

## Choosing a key

The key should be generated once per logical operation on the client side —
typically a UUID — and reused only for retries of that exact operation, never
shared across genuinely different requests.

## Key lifetime

Idempotency keys are honoured for 24 hours from first use. A retry after 24
hours with the same key and same body is treated as a new request rather than
a replay, which is a deliberate trade-off: keeping keys forever would mean the
idempotency store grows without bound.

documents.title: Schema validation errors
documents.body:
## ERR_SCHEMA_VALIDATION

Returned when a request body does not match the documented JSON schema for
that endpoint — a missing required field, a value of the wrong type, or an
enum value outside the documented set.

## Reading the error detail

The error response's `errors` array names the specific field and what was
wrong with it. Point developers here first rather than re-explaining the
whole endpoint's schema — the error already identifies exactly which field
failed and why.

## A common false positive

A client library that has not been updated to the latest API version may send
a field the current schema no longer accepts. Check the API changelog for
recent breaking changes before assuming the integration code itself has a bug.

documents.title: Understanding API error responses
documents.body:
## The standard error shape

Every Ledgerly API error follows the same RFC 7807 problem+json shape: `type`,
`title`, `status`, `errorCode`, `detail`, `instance`, `timestamp` and
`traceId`. Integration code should switch on `errorCode`, never parse
`detail`, which is human-readable prose that may change wording without a
version bump.

## The traceId field

Every error carries a traceId that finds the exact request server-side. When a
developer reports an API error, always ask for the traceId rather than
attempting to reproduce the issue independently — it is the fastest path to
the actual server-side log entry.

documents.title: SDK version compatibility
documents.body:
## Supported SDK versions

Ledgerly supports the current major SDK version and the previous one. An SDK
two major versions behind is not guaranteed compatible with current API
behaviour and may fail in ways that look like a server-side bug but are
actually a client-side schema mismatch.

## Checking a customer's SDK version

Most integration issues reported as "the API changed and broke everything"
trace back to an outdated SDK encountering a schema addition (rarely a
removal — additive changes are the norm) that it was not built to expect.
Confirm the SDK version before escalating to engineering.

documents.title: Diagnosing a webhook delivery failure report
documents.body:
## Steps

1. Pull the webhook delivery log for the endpoint from api-gateway's admin
   panel, filtered to the reported time window.
2. If every attempt shows a non-2xx response from the customer's endpoint,
   this is a customer-side issue — provide the response codes and let them
   investigate their own server.
3. If attempts show a timeout with no response at all, check whether
   Ledgerly's outbound IP range (published in the developer docs) is on the
   customer's firewall allow-list.
4. If delivery genuinely never left api-gateway (no attempts logged at all
   despite the triggering event existing), escalate to platform engineering —
   this is the one pattern that indicates an actual Ledgerly-side bug rather
   than a customer-side integration issue.

documents.title: Handling a suspected rate-limit false positive
documents.body:
## When to use this

A customer reports ERR_RATE_LIMIT while their own logging shows well under the
documented per-minute limit for their plan.

## Steps

1. Pull the RateLimit-Remaining header history for their API key from
   api-gateway's logs across the disputed window.
2. Check for multiple source IPs using the same key — this is the most common
   actual cause, distinct from what the customer believes is happening.
3. If genuinely under the limit with a single consistent source, check for a
   clock skew between the customer's rate-limit tracking and api-gateway's —
   a sliding window measured slightly differently on each side can appear as
   a false positive near the boundary.
4. A confirmed platform-side rate-limiting bug (rare) goes to platform
   engineering with the full request log attached, not a manual limit
   override — overriding masks the bug rather than fixing it.

documents.title: Dashboard slowness troubleshooting
documents.body:
## First questions to ask

Is the slowness affecting one page or the whole product? One specific report
or export, or everything? Since when, and did anything change around that
time (a new integration connected, a much larger data import)?

## ERR_QUERY_TIMEOUT

report-service logs this when a report query exceeds its execution budget,
most often on accounts with an unusually large transaction history combined
with a wide date range selected. Narrowing the date range is the immediate
workaround; the underlying query performance is a platform engineering
concern, not something support resolves directly.

## When it is genuinely global

Widespread slowness across many accounts simultaneously is a platform
incident, not an individual ticket — check the status page and the internal
incident channel before spending time on a single-customer investigation.

documents.title: Report generation delays
documents.body:
## Normal generation time

Most reports generate within 10–15 seconds. A GST return report over a full
financial year with a high transaction volume can take up to 2 minutes — this
is expected, not a fault.

## When a report never completes

report-service marks a generation attempt failed after 5 minutes with
ERR_QUERY_TIMEOUT. If this recurs specifically for one report type on one
account, the likely cause is a data volume the report's query was not sized
for — narrow the date range as an immediate workaround while flagging the
account's data volume to engineering.

## Exports versus reports

An export (a raw data download) and a report (an aggregated view) go through
different code paths in report-service and can fail independently — a working
report does not imply exports will work for the same date range, and vice
versa.

documents.title: Upstream service timeouts
documents.body:
## ERR_UPSTREAM_TIMEOUT

This appears when Ledgerly's own services call another Ledgerly service (for
example, report-service calling ledger-service for transaction data) and that
call exceeds its timeout budget. It is an internal dependency issue, distinct
from ERR_GATEWAY_5XX, which is an external payment gateway failing.

## What it tells you

An upstream timeout on one specific operation, recurring, points at a real
performance issue in the called service under specific conditions (often data
volume) rather than a one-off network blip. A single isolated occurrence with
no recurrence is usually transient and not worth escalating on its own.

## What support can and cannot fix

Support cannot resolve an upstream timeout directly — it requires engineering
to look at the called service's performance. Support's job is to confirm
whether it is isolated or recurring, and to communicate a realistic timeline
rather than a resolution.

documents.title: Browser and device performance factors
documents.body:
## Ruling out the client side first

Before treating slowness as a Ledgerly-side issue, confirm: is this the only
tab open, or are there many? Is the browser up to date? Does the same
slowness occur in a different browser or in incognito mode (which disables
extensions)?

## Extensions are a common cause

Ad blockers and privacy extensions frequently intercept or delay Ledgerly's
own network requests, producing symptoms that look identical to a server-side
performance issue but resolve immediately in incognito mode. This single test
rules out or confirms a large class of "slow" reports in under a minute.

## Older devices and large datasets

An account with a very large transaction history rendering a data-heavy page
(the full ledger view, for instance) genuinely renders slower on older or
lower-memory devices — this is expected client-side rendering cost, not a
server response time issue.

documents.title: Understanding crash and error reports
documents.body:
## What to collect

A crash report is far more actionable with: the exact page or action that
triggered it, the browser and version, and — most valuably — the traceId if
an API error appeared alongside the crash (see the API error response
article for where to find it).

## Reproducibility

A crash that reproduces consistently on a specific action is escalated
differently from one that occurred once and has not recurred — ask the
customer to attempt the same action again before escalating, since a
non-reproducing crash with no traceId gives engineering very little to work
with.

documents.title: Triaging a report of platform-wide slowness
documents.body:
## Steps

1. Check the internal status dashboard and incident channel first — do not
   start an individual investigation if a platform incident is already being
   tracked.
2. If no incident is logged, check whether multiple unrelated tickets are
   reporting the same symptom in the same time window — three or more
   independent reports of slowness within 15 minutes should be flagged to
   platform engineering as a possible undetected incident, even before
   confirming a root cause.
3. For a single ticket with no corroborating reports, proceed with the normal
   dashboard-slowness troubleshooting article rather than assuming a wider
   issue.

documents.title: Escalating a recurring ERR_QUERY_TIMEOUT
documents.body:
## When to escalate

A single occurrence, resolved by narrowing the date range, does not need
escalation. Escalate when the same account hits ERR_QUERY_TIMEOUT on the same
report type more than twice in a month despite the date-range workaround.

## What to include

The account id, the specific report type, the date ranges attempted, and the
account's approximate transaction volume (visible in the account overview
panel). This is the information report-service's owning team needs to decide
whether the account needs a dedicated query optimisation or the account has
simply outgrown the report's current implementation.

documents.title: Tally sync troubleshooting
documents.body:
## ERR_TALLY_CONN

This means sync-service could not establish a connection to the customer's
local Tally instance. Tally sync is a local, on-premises connection — Tally
itself is not cloud software — so this is almost always a network or Tally
configuration issue on the customer's side, not a Ledgerly outage.

## Checklist before escalating

1. Is Tally actually running and the company file open on the machine running
   the Ledgerly sync connector?
2. Is the sync connector's configured port (default 9000) open on the local
   firewall?
3. Was Tally recently updated? A Tally version upgrade can change the local
   API port or require the connector to be reconfigured.

## What sync-service logs

sync-service logs the last successful connection timestamp per account, which
is the fastest way to tell "never connected" (a setup issue) from "was
connected, now is not" (an environment change) — the two have completely
different troubleshooting paths.

documents.title: Zoho Books integration setup
documents.body:
## Connecting Zoho Books

Zoho Books integrates via OAuth, unlike Tally's local connection — the
customer authorises Ledgerly from within their Zoho account, and sync-service
receives a token rather than connecting to anything on the customer's
machine.

## ERR_ZOHO_AUTH_EXPIRED

Zoho OAuth tokens expire after 60 days of inactivity (not 60 days from
issuance — an active connection stays authorised indefinitely). This error
means the token has expired and the customer needs to re-authorise from the
integrations page; it is not recoverable without customer action, because
Ledgerly cannot silently re-request access.

## What syncs and how often

Invoices, contacts and payment records sync every 15 minutes once connected.
A customer who just connected and does not see data yet should be told to
wait for the next sync cycle rather than assuming the connection failed.

documents.title: Bank feed connection issues
documents.body:
## ERR_BANK_FEED_STALE

sync-service marks a bank feed stale when it has not received new transaction
data from the banking data provider for more than 48 hours, which almost
always means the underlying bank-side authorisation has lapsed rather than a
sync-service problem.

## Resolving a stale feed

The customer needs to re-authenticate the bank connection from the bank feeds
settings page — this re-establishes the provider-side authorisation. Ledgerly
cannot refresh a bank connection on the customer's behalf; the re-auth must
happen through the customer's own banking credentials.

## Feed limits by plan

FREE supports one bank feed, PRO up to five, ENTERPRISE unlimited — see the
plan comparison article. A customer wanting to connect an additional feed
beyond their plan's limit will not see an error; the connection option is
simply not offered in the UI.

documents.title: Sync mapping errors
documents.body:
## ERR_SYNC_MAPPING

This appears when a record from the connected system (Tally or Zoho) cannot
be matched to the corresponding Ledgerly record during sync — most often a
customer or vendor name that differs slightly between the two systems (extra
whitespace, a different legal-name format).

## Resolving a mapping error

The sync log names the specific unmapped record. The customer can create a
manual mapping from the sync settings page, which sync-service then reuses
for all future syncs of that same external record — this is a one-time fix
per mismatched record, not a recurring task.

## Preventing future mapping errors

Advise customers to keep customer and vendor names as close to identical as
possible between Ledgerly and their connected system; sync-service's matching
is close but not identical-string matching, and large naming discrepancies
will always need a manual mapping.

documents.title: Choosing between Tally and Zoho integration
documents.body:
## When a customer asks which to use

This is determined by what accounting software the business already uses, not
a Ledgerly preference — Ledgerly does not replace either, it synchronises
with whichever the business already runs day to day.

## Running both

A business using both Tally (for statutory books) and Zoho (for day-to-day
invoicing) can connect both integrations simultaneously; sync-service treats
them as independent connections and does not attempt to reconcile Tally data
against Zoho data or vice versa.

documents.title: Sync failure notifications
documents.body:
## How Ledgerly reports a sync failure

A failed sync attempt (any ERR_SYNC_MAPPING, ERR_TALLY_CONN or
ERR_ZOHO_AUTH_EXPIRED) triggers an email to the account's admin within 15
minutes, and a persistent banner on the sync settings page until resolved.

## Repeated failure notifications

If the same failure email arrives repeatedly despite the customer believing
they fixed it, the most likely cause is the fix not being fully applied — for
Tally, this often means the connector was reconfigured but not restarted; for
Zoho, that re-authorisation was started but not completed through to Zoho's
own consent screen.

documents.title: Diagnosing a persistent ERR_TALLY_CONN report
documents.body:
## Steps

1. Confirm the customer's Tally version against the supported version list
   (in the internal integrations wiki) — an unsupported version is a known
   root cause that has no fix beyond upgrading Tally itself.
2. Ask for the connector's local log file (the customer can export it from
   the connector's system tray icon) rather than relying on a description of
   the symptom.
3. A log showing repeated connection refused (not timeout) almost always
   means the local firewall or antivirus is blocking the connector — this is
   outside Ledgerly's control to fix remotely.
4. A log showing timeout rather than refused suggests Tally itself is not
   responding, which points back to whether Tally and the company file are
   actually open and idle (not mid-operation) on the customer's machine.

documents.title: Export troubleshooting
documents.body:
## ERR_EXPORT_INCOMPLETE

report-service marks an export incomplete when it terminates before writing
every expected row — most commonly a timeout on a very large date range, the
same underlying cause as ERR_QUERY_TIMEOUT on reports.

## Confirming a genuinely missing row

Before treating a report as buggy, confirm the specific missing entry exists
in the main ledger view for that date — an entry created very close to the
export's cutoff timestamp can legitimately fall just outside the exported
window depending on timezone handling, which is expected rather than an
error.

## Workaround for large exports

Splitting a large export into smaller date-range chunks (monthly instead of
annual, for instance) avoids the timeout and is the standard workaround while
any underlying performance issue is investigated separately.

documents.title: GST return reconciliation
documents.body:
## ERR_GST_RECONCILE_FAIL

This appears when Ledgerly's GST return generation cannot reconcile the
account's recorded transactions against the GSTIN-linked GSTR-2A/2B data
fetched from the GST portal — usually because of a mismatch between an
invoice's recorded GSTIN and the one on the portal's records for the same
transaction.

## Resolving a reconciliation failure

The reconciliation report names the specific invoices that failed to match.
The customer needs to verify the GSTIN entered against that transaction is
correct — a single-digit GSTIN typo is by far the most common cause and
explains the large majority of reconciliation failures reported.

## What this does not affect

A reconciliation failure affects only the GST return generation for the
mismatched invoices specifically; it does not affect the underlying ledger
entries, which remain correct regardless of GST reconciliation status.

documents.title: Missing or duplicate records
documents.body:
## Investigating a missing record

Ask for the exact date, amount and counterparty of the missing entry. Check
ledger-service directly for a matching record before assuming it was never
created — the far more common cause of an apparently "missing" record is a
filter on the current view (a date range, a category filter) hiding an entry
that does exist.

## Investigating a duplicate

A genuine duplicate ledger entry (not just an entry appearing twice in a
report view, which is usually a rendering issue) requires checking whether it
originated from two separate sync events — see the sync mapping article — or
was manually entered twice by the customer.

## Never delete without confirmation

A record believed to be a duplicate must be confirmed with the customer
before deletion. Financial records that look duplicate can represent two
genuinely separate transactions (a customer paying twice for two different
invoices with the same amount, for instance).

documents.title: Data export formats
documents.body:
## Supported formats

Ledgerly exports data as CSV, XLSX, or a GST-portal-ready JSON for return
filing. PDF is available for individual invoices and reports but not for bulk
transaction exports.

## Choosing the right format for accounting software import

XLSX preserves number formatting that CSV does not (leading zeros in
reference numbers, for instance, which CSV can silently strip) — always
recommend XLSX over CSV for a customer planning to import the export into
another accounting tool.

documents.title: Understanding report date ranges and timezones
documents.body:
## How date ranges are applied

Every report and export in Ledgerly applies its date range in the account's
configured timezone (set in account settings), not UTC and not the browser's
local timezone. A transaction timestamped just before or after midnight can
appear in a different day's report than expected if the account timezone is
misconfigured.

## Diagnosing a suspected off-by-one-day issue

Confirm the account's configured timezone matches the business's actual
location. A business operating in IST with the account still on the default
UTC setting will see transactions from the last few hours of each IST day
appear in the following day's report.

documents.title: Data retention and historical access
documents.body:
## How long data is retained

Transaction and ledger data is retained indefinitely regardless of plan tier
or subscription status — even a downgraded FREE account retains full
historical access to data created while on a paid plan.

## Accessing very old data

Reports default to the last 90 days for performance reasons, but any
historical range can be explicitly selected — data is never deleted or
archived out of reach, only out of the default view.

documents.title: Investigating a GST reconciliation failure pattern
documents.body:
## When this applies

Multiple ERR_GST_RECONCILE_FAIL entries for one account across many invoices,
rather than a single isolated mismatch.

## Steps

1. Export the reconciliation failure list from report-service's admin panel.
2. Check whether the failures cluster around a specific counterparty GSTIN —
   a single wrong GSTIN reused across many invoices (common when a customer
   copies an old invoice as a template) explains most bulk-failure cases at
   once.
3. If failures are scattered across many different GSTINs with no pattern,
   check whether the GST portal itself had a known outage during the affected
   period — a portal-side sync gap looks identical to individual GSTIN errors
   from Ledgerly's side.

documents.title: Handling a bulk export performance escalation
documents.body:
## Steps

1. Confirm the exact export type, date range, and account transaction volume
   from the failed export's log entry.
2. Recommend the date-range-splitting workaround immediately while
   investigating — the customer should not be left waiting on an
   investigation before getting a usable export.
3. Escalate to report-service's owning team only if the same account hits
   ERR_EXPORT_INCOMPLETE even on a single-month range, which indicates a
   genuine performance problem rather than simply a large total dataset.

documents.title: KYC document requirements
documents.body:
## What is required

A PAN card and one business proof document (GST certificate, Udyam
registration, or a partnership deed for non-GST-registered businesses) are
required for every account above FREE tier. Sole proprietors without GST
registration can use a bank statement showing business transactions as an
alternative business proof.

## ERR_KYC_DOC_REJECT

kyc-service rejects a document automatically when the uploaded image is
illegible, the document type does not match what was selected, or the
document has visibly expired (relevant for some business registration
certificates that carry a validity date).

## Resubmission

A rejected document can be re-uploaded immediately from the same onboarding
screen; there is no cooldown period and no limit on resubmission attempts.

documents.title: GSTIN verification issues
documents.body:
## ERR_GSTIN_INVALID

kyc-service validates a submitted GSTIN's format (15 characters, matching the
state-code-plus-PAN-plus-checksum structure) and, separately, verifies it
against the GST portal's registry. This error can mean either a format
problem or a portal-verification failure, and the two need different fixes.

## Format errors

A format error is almost always a transcription mistake — ask the customer to
copy-paste directly from their GST certificate rather than typing it.

## Portal verification failures

A correctly formatted GSTIN that still fails portal verification usually
means the registration is very recent and has not yet propagated to the
lookup Ledgerly queries, or the registration status is anything other than
"Active" (cancelled, suspended, or under cancellation) on the GST portal
itself.

documents.title: PAN verification mismatches
documents.body:
## ERR_PAN_MISMATCH

This occurs when the PAN submitted during KYC does not match the name
provided elsewhere in the application — kyc-service checks the PAN against
the income-tax database's registered name, and a business name that differs
from the PAN-registered legal name (a trade name used instead of the
registered name, commonly) triggers this.

## Resolving it

The customer needs to enter the legal name exactly as registered against
their PAN, not their trade name or brand name. This is a common source of
friction for businesses that operate primarily under a trade name different
from their formal registration.

documents.title: Account setup checklist
documents.body:
## The full onboarding sequence

1. Basic business details (name, address, industry).
2. KYC document upload (see the KYC requirements article).
3. GSTIN entry and verification, if applicable.
4. Bank feed connection (optional at setup, can be added later).
5. Team member invitations, if applicable.

## What blocks account activation

Only step 2 (KYC) is strictly required before the account can process any
real transactions — steps 3–5 can be completed later, and a customer stuck on
GSTIN verification should be told they can proceed with basic invoicing
immediately once KYC clears, without waiting for GST setup to complete.

documents.title: Business verification timeline
documents.body:
## How long verification takes

KYC document review is typically completed within 24 hours of a valid
submission. A submission stuck beyond 48 hours with no rejection and no
approval should be escalated — this indicates the review queue itself has a
problem, not that the customer's specific documents are unusually complex.

## What happens during the wait

The account is fully created and accessible during KYC review; only specific
actions (sending invoices to real customers, connecting live bank feeds) are
gated behind verification completing. The customer can explore the product
and set up their chart of accounts while waiting.

documents.title: Team member invitations during onboarding
documents.body:
## Inviting team members

Team member invitations can be sent from account settings once the primary
account holder's own KYC has cleared — a team member's individual access does
not require separate KYC, only the business-level verification.

## Invitation link expiry

An invitation link expires after 7 days. An expired invitation must be
resent, not resubmitted — the original link cannot be reactivated once
expired, a new one must be generated.

documents.title: Escalating a stuck KYC review
documents.body:
## When to escalate

A submission with no ERR_KYC_DOC_REJECT and no approval after 48 hours.

## Steps

1. Confirm from kyc-service's admin panel that the submission is actually in
   the review queue and not stuck in an upload-processing state (rare, but
   distinguishable — an upload-processing stall shows no reviewer assignment
   at all, where a genuine queue delay shows an assigned reviewer with no
   completed decision).
2. For a queue delay, escalate to the KYC review team with the account id and
   submission timestamp — do not attempt to expedite by re-uploading, which
   creates a duplicate submission and can reset queue position.
3. For an upload-processing stall, ask the customer to re-upload; this is a
   one-time processing glitch, not a queue issue, and resubmission resolves
   it directly.

documents.title: Verifying a disputed KYC rejection
documents.body:
## When this applies

A customer disputes an ERR_KYC_DOC_REJECT they believe was incorrect — the
document was legible and correctly typed in their view.

## Steps

1. Pull the actual submitted document image from kyc-service's admin panel
   and review it directly rather than taking the customer's description at
   face value.
2. Check the specific rejection reason code, not just that a rejection
   occurred — kyc-service records which check failed (illegibility, type
   mismatch, or expiry).
3. A genuinely incorrect automated rejection (document is clearly legible and
   correctly typed) is escalated to the KYC review team for manual override —
   agents cannot override an automated KYC rejection directly.

documents.title: UPI refund vs reversal terminology
documents.body:
## Two different words for related outcomes

Agents and customers often use "refund" and "reversal" interchangeably, but
payment-service distinguishes them: a reversal undoes a payment that was
debited but never successfully completed on Ledgerly's side (see the UPI
payment failures article). A refund returns money for a payment that did
complete successfully, initiated afterward -- a cancelled order, for
instance.

## Why the distinction matters to a customer

A reversal happens automatically once ERR_UPI_COLLECT_FAILED or a similar
failure is detected; a refund requires an explicit request or business action
(cancelling an order) before it is initiated. Telling a customer "your refund
is being processed" for what is actually an automatic reversal sets an
inaccurate expectation about who needs to do what next.

documents.title: Recognising a phishing attempt targeting Ledgerly customers
documents.body:
## What Ledgerly never asks for

Ledgerly never asks for a customer's password, OTP, or full card number over
email, phone or chat -- support can see account details but never the
customer's actual credentials, because auth-service stores only hashed
passwords and kyc-service redacts card numbers to the last four digits
everywhere they appear.

## Common phishing patterns reported by customers

Emails claiming a subscription payment failed and demanding immediate card
re-entry via an external link, or messages claiming a large "cashback" is
pending release. Genuine Ledgerly billing emails always link to the
in-product billing page, never to a third-party payment form.

## What to tell a customer who reports one

Confirm the email did not come from a ledgerly.com address, advise them not
to click any links in it, and forward the phishing email to the security
team via the internal report-phishing address.

documents.title: Multi-currency limitations
documents.body:
## Current currency support

Ledgerly currently supports INR only for both collection and subscription
billing. A customer asking about multi-currency invoicing should be told
this is not currently supported, rather than given a workaround that will
not actually function correctly.

## Why this comes up

Customers occasionally attempt to enter a foreign-currency amount in an
invoice field expecting automatic conversion; Ledgerly treats any numeric
entry as INR regardless of any currency symbol typed alongside it, which can
produce a wildly incorrect invoice amount if not caught early.

documents.title: Understanding two-factor recovery codes
documents.body:
## What recovery codes are for

When 2FA is enabled, auth-service generates ten single-use recovery codes,
shown once at setup. Each one can be used in place of a TOTP code if the
customer loses access to their authenticator app, without going through the
full identity-verification 2FA reset process.

## When recovery codes are exhausted

Once all ten are used, the customer must go through the standard 2FA reset
verification (see the identity verification runbook) -- recovery codes are
not regenerated automatically, and a customer who saved them somewhere
insecure should be advised to reset 2FA proactively rather than wait until
locked out.

documents.title: API pagination
documents.body:
## How list endpoints paginate

Every Ledgerly API list endpoint returns a cursor-based page: a data array
and a pagination object with nextCursor and hasNext. There is no
page-number parameter -- cursor pagination is used throughout because the
underlying data changes while a client may be paging through it.

## Common integration mistakes

Constructing a cursor manually instead of passing back exactly what
nextCursor returned is the most common integration bug reported -- the
cursor is an opaque token and must be round-tripped unmodified, never
parsed or reconstructed by the client.

documents.title: Deprecated API endpoint migration
documents.body:
## Currently deprecated endpoints

The v0 invoice creation endpoint is deprecated in favour of the current v1
endpoint and will stop accepting new integrations from a published sunset
date, though existing integrations continue to function until then.

## Identifying deprecated usage

A Deprecation response header appears on every call to a deprecated
endpoint, naming the replacement. Point developers at this header directly
rather than requiring them to check documentation separately.

documents.title: Dashboard widget customisation
documents.body:
## What can be customised

The dashboard's summary widgets (revenue, outstanding invoices, recent
activity) can be reordered and individually hidden from account settings.
This is purely a display preference and does not affect any underlying data
or report accuracy.

## A common support confusion

A customer who has hidden a widget sometimes reports the underlying data as
"missing" rather than recognising it as a display preference -- confirm
whether the data is absent from the full report view (a real issue) or only
from the dashboard summary (a display setting) before investigating further.

documents.title: Mobile app feature parity
documents.body:
## What the mobile app supports

The Ledgerly mobile app supports invoice creation, payment collection
status, and basic reporting. It does not currently support bank feed
configuration, Tally/Zoho integration setup, or team member management --
those remain web-only.

## Setting expectations

A customer trying to complete an integration setup from the mobile app
should be redirected to the web app rather than troubleshooting a feature
that does not exist there; this is a common source of "it's broken" reports
that are actually "not available here yet."

documents.title: Handling a request to merge two accounts
documents.body:
## When this comes up

A customer who signed up twice, or two customers who registered a business
that should be one account, occasionally ask to merge accounts.

## Current limitation

Account merging is not currently supported as a self-service or agent
action -- each account's transaction history, KYC verification and billing
state are tied to its account id in a way that cannot be safely combined
without risking duplicate or lost financial records.

## What to offer instead

Recommend the customer choose one account to continue using and manually
re-enter any data unique to the other, rather than promising a merge that
cannot currently be delivered.

documents.title: Explaining the audit trail feature
documents.body:
## What is logged

Every status change, assignment, priority change and message on a
ticket-like record is logged with a timestamp and, where applicable, who
made the change -- this is the same append-only pattern used for Ledgerly's
own support ticketing internally, and PRO/ENTERPRISE accounts get an
equivalent audit trail for their own team's actions within the product
(invoice edits, user permission changes).

## Why it cannot be edited

The audit trail is intentionally immutable -- even an admin cannot edit or
delete a past entry, because an editable audit trail defeats its own
purpose as a record of what actually happened.

documents.title: Password strength requirements
documents.body:
## Current requirements

A Ledgerly password must be at least 12 characters. There is no requirement
for a specific mix of character types (uppercase, digits, symbols) -- length
alone is the enforced control, which auth-service checks against a
commonly-breached-password list rather than arbitrary complexity rules.

## Why length rather than complexity rules

A long passphrase is measurably harder to guess than a short password
forced into an arbitrary complexity pattern, and complexity rules are well
known to push people toward predictable substitutions (like a 1 for an I)
that do not actually add meaningful strength.

documents.title: Understanding notification preferences
documents.body:
## What can be configured

Email notification preferences (payment received, invoice overdue, sync
failure) can be individually enabled or disabled from account settings.
Security notifications (password changed, new device login) cannot be
disabled -- they are sent regardless of preference settings, deliberately.

## A common request Ledgerly declines

Customers occasionally ask to disable security notifications entirely,
usually because of email volume. This is not offered, because a security
notification a customer cannot see is a security control that does not
function.
